doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Writing for two tenors: Stephen Riley and Ned Gould
summary: Players alter his written parts; he picks pretty notes for two tenors and likes tenor players who avoid sounding like Shorter or Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That’s right. That’s right. A lot of times it’s not. Sometimes it is, usually it’s not. And sometimes it’s better than you thought, and sometimes it’s worse. And like you know I have a sax player who I love who plays in my band sometimes, Stephen Riley. And I’ll write like a song with the harmony. And he usually only plays what I write half the time. And sometimes he just does his own thing. And that usually sometimes sounds a lot better. You know I like to keep it open, you know, because you never know what somebody’ll add to it.

When you’re writing for two tenors, are you like sort of methodical, like all right I’m playing a G sus type bass line and I’m going to give this tenor the third, and this tenor the fifth, or is it a little more just what sounds right. I don’t know if that was a —

No, no, no, no. I know what you’re saying. No for me it’s kind of what sounds right. I mean yeah, I just usually kind of pick notes. Sometimes you know you’ll write a melody and then you’ll go through and harmonize it, try different ways to do it. But it’s really only two voices with the tenors. So I just try to pick pretty notes, really. Sounds kind of simple.
Well that tune was pretty, “The Hempire Strikes Back.”
And it was sort of visual too. I got this sort of visual thing listening to it. And those tenors were matched, they went well together I thought.
I think so too. They both have pretty sounds.
Uh huh. Because you could again, replace one of them, and it probably would change the nature of the music some more.

Totally. I mean those guys, Ned Gould and Stephen Riley, they both have pretty sounds. I mean once again, getting back to the school sound, the school thing, a lot of tenor players, as they should, sound like some amalgamation of Wayne Shorter and John Coltrane you know, which is great. I mean that’s my favorites. But I like guys who maybe sound a little different you know, than those two.
